themes.name: High sensitivity screening models
themes.description: Studies reporting LLMs achieving sensitivity of roughly 90% or higher for title/abstract or full‑text screening, indicating strong ability to identify relevant records.

themes.name: Ensemble and prompt‑optimization approaches
themes.description: Studies that improve performance through prompt engineering, model ensembles, full‑agreement strategies, or calibrated zero‑shot ensembles.

themes.name: Fine‑tuned or specialized LLMs
themes.description: Studies evaluating fine‑tuned, domain‑specific, or compact LLMs and comparing them with general‑purpose models for systematic review screening.

themes.name: Other findings
themes.description: Studies not covered by the themes above.

High sensitivity screening models.narrative: High‑sensitivity screening models using large language models (LLMs) consistently achieve sensitivities at or above 90% in several diagnostic accuracy studies. Li et al. reported overall abstract‑screening sensitivity of 90% (range 90–97%) across two datasets, with specificity varying from 59% to 93% [R0011]. Qiu et al. demonstrated 98% to 100% sensitivity for abstract screening across three independent datasets, with specificity between 80.6% and 93% [R0079]. The Review Copilot system achieved 99.2% sensitivity for title/abstract screening across four systematic reviews, albeit with lower specificity (83.6%) [R0049]. In contrast, studies using alternative LLMs reported more modest sensitivities: Oami et al. observed a modified‑prompt sensitivity of 0.91 after optimisation, while the original prompt yielded 0.75 [R0010]; Ramchandani et al. found peri‑operative recall of 0.89 but pre‑operative recall of 0.67 [R0014]; López‑Pineda et al. reported 77.5% sensitivity for Llama 3 and 56.2% for ChatGPT‑4o mini [R0037]; and Yamoah et al. achieved 88% sensitivity with a dual‑reviewer reference standard on a large sample of 15,307 abstracts [R0073]. Additional evidence from benchmark testing showed ChatGPT v4.0 reaching 93% sensitivity on the Bannach‑Brown database [R0035], and a fine‑tuned 1.2 B‑parameter model attaining 91.18% sensitivity on 8,277 records [R0096]. Across studies, higher sensitivities are associated with prompt optimisation, larger LLM versions (e.g., GPT‑4), and thorough dual‑reviewer reference standards, though specificity often declines when sensitivity is maximised.
High sensitivity screening models.certainty_rationale: Evidence is primarily from observational diagnostic accuracy studies with some concerns for bias and inconsistent reference standards, leading to downgrades for risk of bias and inconsistency.

Ensemble and prompt‑optimization approac.narrative: Ensemble and prompt‑optimization strategies consistently improve LLM screening performance. Oami et al. reported that using a chain‑of‑thought prompt raised integrated sensitivity from 0.75 to 0.91 while specificity stayed at 0.98 in a sample of 16,669 records [R0010]. Sanghera et al. found that zero‑shot prompting combined with optimal prompt selection achieved up to 100% sensitivity on a balanced development set and maintained high sensitivity (0.756‑1.00) on 119,695 records, with LLM‑human ensembles reaching perfect sensitivity and higher precision than single models [R0025]. Guo et al. showed that a GPT‑based prompt including screening criteria yielded 0.91 overall accuracy and a κ of 0.96 versus human consensus on 24,307 abstracts, outperforming human interrater agreement (κ = 0.46) [R0028]. Hilkenmeier et al. demonstrated that requiring full agreement across three LLMs produced precision 0.88, recall 0.96, specificity 0.87 and F1 0.92, surpassing prior single‑LLM results [R0061]. Wang et al. confirmed that calibrated ensembles of zero‑shot generative LLMs outperformed individual models in work‑saved‑screening and precision across five test collections [R0138]. Godhwani et al. observed that an actor‑critic configuration improved calibration and discrimination compared with single‑model setups, highlighting the benefit of advanced prompting frameworks [R0103]. Wilkins reported that chain‑of‑thought prompting with GPT‑4 achieved 71% sensitivity, 89% specificity and 84% accuracy, comparable to an alternative zero‑shot approach, indicating modest gains from prompt variation [R0145].
Ensemble and prompt‑optimization approac.certainty_rationale: Evidence is observational diagnostic accuracy studies with some risk of bias and inconsistency across datasets, leading to downgrades for bias and indirectness.

Fine‑tuned or specialized LLMs.narrative: Fine‑tuned, domain‑specific LLMs appear to achieve higher accuracy than general‑purpose models for title and abstract screening. In a single‑disease review of 1,030 records, the fine‑tuned UveAItis model reached 93.3% accuracy, an AUC of 0.887, sensitivity of 81.7% and specificity of 95.7%, outperforming GPT‑4o (AUC 0.805) and Claude Sonnet 3.5 (AUC 0.669) [R0069]. A larger diagnostic study of 8,277 records showed that fine‑tuning a 1.2 B‑parameter LLM raised weighted F1 by 80.79% and yielded 86.4% overall agreement with a human coder, with sensitivity 91.18% and specificity 86.38% [R0096]. Across three reviews (7,693–21,116 records), compact models using structured prompts achieved up to 100% sensitivity but low precision (<10%); balanced accuracy varied from 76.7% to 91.3% and specificity reached 92.7% for the best model [R0072]. In contrast, a non‑fine‑tuned GPT‑4 evaluation reported accuracy comparable to humans but noted variability due to dataset imbalance and chance agreement, without any fine‑tuning [R0045]. A comparative study of six reviews found that the zero‑shot Llama‑3.1‑8B‑Instruct LLM matched human recall but had lower specificity than traditional supervised classifiers, highlighting a trade‑off between sensitivity and specificity for untuned models [R0058]. Finally, a preliminary diagnostic study of 811 publications found GPT‑4 to have the highest screening accuracy among tested models, though the study relied on prompt engineering rather than fine‑tuning and provided limited detail on bias [R0085]. Overall, fine‑tuned models consistently show superior balanced performance, while general‑purpose LLMs exhibit more variable results that depend on prompting strategy and dataset characteristics.
Fine‑tuned or specialized LLMs.certainty_rationale: Evidence is mainly from observational diagnostic studies with some concerns of bias and limited generalisability; inconsistency across models and datasets leads to downgrading, but effect sizes are sizable.

Other findings.narrative: In a prospective diagnostic study, LLM‑assisted title and abstract screening achieved a pooled sensitivity of 0.73 (95% CI 0.57‑0.85) and a specificity of 0.99 (95% CI 0.97‑0.99), yielding an AUC of 0.97 (95% CI 0.96‑0.99) when compared with dual independent human reviewers as the reference standard [R0018]. Post‑hoc prompt revisions markedly improved sensitivity to 0.98 (95% CI 0.74‑1.00) while preserving high specificity (0.98, 95% CI 0.94‑0.99), indicating that prompt engineering can substantially affect performance [R0018]. For full‑text screening, the same LLMs showed sensitivity of 0.87 (95% CI 0.77‑0.99) and specificity of 0.96 (95% CI 0.91‑0.98), with an AUC of 0.96 (95% CI 0.94‑0.97), suggesting comparable accuracy to manual screening across both stages [R0018]. The study also reported that LLMs outperformed traditional machine‑learning tools such as ASReview (sensitivity 0.58) and Abstrackr (sensitivity 0.48), highlighting a potential advantage of large language models over earlier algorithms [R0018]. However, the authors noted a key limitation: the use of previously published systematic reviews may overlap with LLM training data, introducing selection bias and possibly inflating performance estimates [R0018]. The evidence rests on a single full‑text report with some concerns for bias, and sample size details were not provided, limiting precision.
Other findings.certainty_rationale: Observational diagnostic design with some risk of bias (training data overlap) and imprecision due to missing sample size; inconsistency not evident but indirectness and bias lead to downgrading.

discussion.summary_of_evidence: The 21 diagnostic accuracy studies show that large language models (LLMs) can achieve high sensitivity for title and abstract screening, often exceeding 90% when prompt optimisation, ensemble methods, or fine‑tuning are applied. High‑sensitivity models such as those reported by Li et al. and Qiu et al. reached 90–100% sensitivity, though specificity varied widely (59–93%) [R0011,R0079,R0049]. Ensemble and prompt‑optimisation strategies consistently improved performance, with chain‑of‑thought or zero‑shot prompting raising recall while maintaining or improving precision [R0010,R0025,R0028,R0061,R0138,R0103,R0145]. Fine‑tuned, domain‑specific LLMs demonstrated superior balanced accuracy compared with general‑purpose models, achieving sensitivities around 81–91% and specificities up to 96% [R0069,R0096,R0072,R0045,R0058,R0085]. A prospective study reported pooled sensitivity of 0.73 and specificity of 0.99, which improved to 0.98 sensitivity after prompt revision, suggesting that engineering choices markedly affect outcomes [R0018]. Across themes, the evidence is moderate in certainty due to observational designs, some risk of bias, and heterogeneity in reference standards.
discussion.limitations_of_evidence: Most studies were observational diagnostic accuracy designs with some concerns for bias, such as unblinded reference standards, single‑reviewer coding, or potential overlap between training data and test sets, which may inflate performance estimates [R0018,R0011,R0079]. Reference standards varied (dual‑reviewer, single‑reviewer, or consensus), limiting comparability. Sample sizes and reporting of confidence intervals were inconsistent, reducing precision for some estimates. The heterogeneity of LLM versions, prompting strategies, and datasets introduces indirectness, and few studies evaluated full‑text screening or real‑world workflow integration, restricting generalisability.
discussion.implications: Practitioners should view LLMs as promising tools that can achieve high sensitivity in title/abstract screening when carefully optimised, but they should not replace human reviewers without validation in the specific review context. Future research should employ blinded, multi‑reviewer reference standards, report detailed performance metrics, and assess LLMs across diverse topics and full‑text screening stages. Comparative studies of fine‑tuned versus zero‑shot models, and investigations of ensemble approaches in real‑time systematic review workflows, will help clarify the conditions under which LLMs can reliably augment or replace manual screening.

rationale: Automated title‑and‑abstract screening is widely promoted as a way to lessen the labour‑intensive workload of systematic reviews, yet the empirical evidence for large language models (LLMs) in this role remains fragmented. Several recent investigations have begun to evaluate LLMs for screening, reporting mixed accuracy and highlighting the need for systematic synthesis of comparative performance data [R0108]. Early work has demonstrated that fine‑tuned, smaller LLMs can be promising for large‑scale reviews, but these studies have been limited to single models or specific domains [R0096]. More comprehensive assessments have emerged, testing state‑of‑the‑art models such as GPT‑4 and GPT‑4o Mini against human reviewers and reporting sensitivity, specificity, and workload reductions across thousands of records and multiple clinical topics [R0045, R0028, R0072]. Nonetheless, direct head‑to‑head comparisons between LLMs and traditional supervised machine‑learning baselines are scarce, and the methodological quality of existing reports varies, making it difficult for reviewers to gauge reliability and to decide whether to adopt LLMs in practice [R0058]. A systematic review that aggregates these heterogeneous findings will clarify the current accuracy of LLM‑assisted screening, identify conditions under which LLMs approach or exceed human performance, and pinpoint gaps that future research must address.

revision_issues.description: Unsupported statement: "Overall, studies using dual‑reviewer reference standards and larger sample sizes (e.g., Oami, Li, Qiu) report higher sensitivities, whereas smaller or single‑reviewer designs (e.g., Yamoah) show modestly lower values." — The evidence contradicts this comparison. Yamoah et al. [R0073] used a dual-reviewer reference standard (with a third for consensus) and reported a sensitivity of up to 89% (or 88% in effects), which is not 'modestly lower' than the 90-100% range reported by Qiu et al. [R0079] (who used human reviewers as reference, details on independence not explicitly stated as dual in the card but implied by 'human reviewers') or Li et al. [R0011]. Furthermore, Yamoah's sample size (15,307) is larger than Li [R0011] (3,715) and Qiu [R0079] (1,000-1,500), so the claim that 'larger sample sizes... report higher sensitivities' while citing Yamoah as a 'smaller... design' is factually incorrect regarding the sample size comparison. The claim also incorrectly groups Yamoah with 'single-reviewer designs' when the evidence states 'Dual independent reviewers'.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Remove the comparative claim about sample size and reviewer type correlating with sensitivity, or correct it to reflect that Yamoah et al. used a dual-reviewer standard and a large sample size (15,307) but reported a sensitivity (88-89%) that was comparable to or slightly lower than the highest-performing models in other studies, without mischaracterizing the sample size or reviewer process.

revision_issues.description: Unsupported statement: "In Oami et al., modifying the prompt raised integrated sensitivity from 0.75 to 0.91 while specificity remained above 0.98, demonstrating the impact of prompt engineering on a dataset of 16,670 records [R0010]." — The number of records is incorrect. The evidence states the sample size was 16,669 records, not 16,670.

"LLMs can reliably identify relevant records in systematic‑review screening, often meeting the 90% sensitivity threshold" — The thematic synthesis rates the certainty of evidence for high-sensitivity models as 'low' and notes significant variability (sensitivities ranging from 56% to 100%). The term 'reliably' implies a level of consistency and confidence that is not supported by the low certainty rating and the wide performance range.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Soften the language to reflect the low certainty and variability, e.g., 'LLMs show potential to identify relevant records, with some models meeting the 90% sensitivity threshold, but performance is variable and certainty of evidence is low.'

revision_issues.description: "Overall, evidence suggests LLMs can reliably identify relevant records" — Similar to the abstract, this conclusion overstates the certainty of the evidence. The synthesis explicitly states 'Certainty: low' for the high-sensitivity theme and highlights risk-of-bias concerns (unblinded reference standards, single-reviewer coding) that 'temper confidence'. 'Reliably' is too strong a claim given the methodological limitations and low certainty.
revision_issues.suggested_fix: Change to 'evidence suggests LLMs have the potential to identify relevant records' or 'LLMs can identify relevant records with high sensitivity in specific contexts', acknowledging the low certainty and methodological constraints.
